I'm not an expert on this, so if there are inaccuracies in what I have just written, just let me know.

Also, high efficiency solar panels use metals of which there isn't that much abundance of,

This is a common misconception. The metals in question are "rare earths" which are called that for historic reasons not because they are actually rare. It is true that mining them in efficient ways is difficult, but abundance is not an issue. See e.g. here. Unfortunately, they are used in a variety of other electronics so the demand is very high.

Note also that we're getting better at recycling solar panels, but more of the current work is focused on making them have long lifespans rather than making them easier to recycle.

If the solar power is made with mirror arrays, then it is very renewable and actually quite environmentally friendly.

Agreed. Unfortunately, mirror systems generally need to be regular power plants rather than things like individual roof systems, so they take away some of the advantages of solar. Note that some countries (such as in some parts of Israel) use solar power with mirrors as hot water heaters on roofs for regular hot water use. But that's not efficient work in most of the US. (People need to get up early before sunrise much of the year, the external temperature is not very hot, and the total number of daylight hours during winter is very low.)

solar arrays also have the problem that clouds make the rays from the sun scatter too much, making them mainly effective in places with many days with almost completely no clouds, and those places often are dry, which will cause dust and sand storms which will damage the mirrors. In Italy and Spain I know that they are quite effective. For the problem you're mentioning, using hydro power dams with reversible turbines can be a solution. (pumping water up when there is surplus, and sending it back down when there is a shortage)

Processed sugars are good? ORLY. Please explain.

I did NOT say processed sugars are good; I said they are not bad. Good and bad are relative terms, which are easy for people to understand, so often it's understood or taught this way, but it's wrong.

The battle against processed sugar is based on

  1. Excessive carb consumption
  2. Fructose consumption (the metabolism of fructose is different, and apparently more limited in more than one way than glucose's metabolism)
  3. Empty calories, meaning calories without any other nutritional value, like vitamins.
  4. Sudden increase of blood glucose

I'm going to disregard #4 right now, because that only has an implication for diabetics and people who have trouble controlling their hunger (and even in the second case it's not that bad). I used to take really good care of avoiding #4, but stopped after I found out, both in paper and personally, that in a healthy individual the sudden insulin secretion might actually be good for multiple reasons, such as an increase of serotonin or alertness.

1 is not a problem of sugar being processed or not, it's a matter of looking at the label and seeing how many carbs the product has and fitting it in your diet. If you'll go over your daily limit, don't eat it, it's that simply. I do understand some people have trouble with holding back from eating though, but then the problem is not the sugar, but the habit.

2 Fructose is not bad per-se (and it's probably unavoidable), and in small amounts there's no data that supports it being damaging. Now, don't get me wrong, there isn't enough research on fructose to make specific conclusions, like saying exactly how much is fine, and depending on the source I have seen this go from 20g to 80g. Fructose does have at least one researched thing against it, and it's that instead of satiating hunger it makes you hungrier, so it makes it harder to keep the amount of calories controlled. Table sugar is 50:50 fructose:glucose, high fructose corn syrup usually consumed goes has 42%-55% fructose according to wikipedia, and that's similar to the ratio found in fruits like in bananas or honey which are 'natural' products. Not all fruits have much fructose, so the problem in this case is not if it's processed or not, but how much fructose you're getting, and should be managed on a case-by-case basis with each food if you're worried about it.

3 Empty calories are only a concern if you're not getting enough non-caloric nutrients. You don't need a multivitamin either, just eating different colored veggies through the day is a good rule of thumb, these things are really frigging loaded with nutrients and are amazingly low in calories. Seriously! check broccoli's nutrients, it's glorious.

Saying "avoid processed sugars/foods" is a good general advice, because processed sugar/foods generally slant nutrient consumption against concerns 1-4, and the average joe has a hard time figuring how to get a decent nutrient intake, however it's perfectly safe to consume a high percentage of your calories from processed foods IF YOU KNOW WHAT YOU'RE DOING. However, saying "processed food is bad" is not advice, or true, just like saying 'natural is good' is not true either, there's plenty of 'natural' stuff that can kill you from a single dose when consumed.

I don't know of any other valid concerns regarding processed sugar, but if there are I'm interested in knowing about them.
